articles.title: Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek' captain and 'X-Men' star, dies at 86
articles.summary: Patrick Stewart, a revered English actor best known for his work on Star Trek , has died. He was 86. According to a post on his X account , Stewart died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles "in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," the post read. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace. "His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre. He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction's most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise," the post continued. "His professional accomplishments were humbly matched by his philanthropy and activism on behalf of human rights, survivors of domestic violence, global refugees, veterans' mental health services, and animal welfare, particularly his cherished foster puppies. Read more from Yahoo: Live reaction and tributes to the life and legacy of Patrick Stewart "He was a Knight, Chancellor, motor sport enthusiast, and lifelong Huddersfield Football fan," the post added. "He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion, and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life." In lieu of flowers, memorial contributions may be made to: Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund https://t.co/luC5CdcWDy Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources https://t.co/zvNptfyuNd Photo Credit: Tommy Garcia pic.twitter.com/XNncEVq56X — Patrick Stewart (@SirPatStew) October 29, 2026 Born on July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, Yorkshire, England, Stewart dropped out of school at age 15 to work as a reporter at a local newspaper and then furniture salesman before enrolling in drama school in 1957. He made his professional theater debut in 1959, eventually joining the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. He spent the next two decades performing in both classical and contemporary productions — Edward Albee's Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? ; Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra — alongside fellow stage greats such as Ben Kingsley and Helen Mirren. In the mid '80s, Stewart moved to Los Angeles to star in Star Trek: The Next Generation , which ran from 1987 to 1994, as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. Also see: From Shakespeare to Picard and Professor X, Patrick Stewart was a legend long before Hollywood. See his life in photos. He later reprised the role on the big screen for a series of Star Trek films, including Star Trek: Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998) and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002). Stewart had more than 160 credits as an actor, according to IMDB , most recently as the voice of Avery Bullock on the animated comedy series American Dad!. He will also appear posthumously in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday as Professor Charles Xavier, a role he played in several previous X-Men films. Related: Patrick Stewart will return as Professor X in 'Avengers: Doomsday,' nearly 2 months after his death In 2010, Stewart was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II and given the title of Sir in honor of his contributions to TV, film and theater. "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today," Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside Stewart in X-Men , wrote in an Instagram post . "And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days." The Royal Shakespeare Company wrote on Instagram that Stewart was "a colossus of both stage and screen and one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation." And William Shatner, who preceded Stewart as captain of Star Trek 's USS Enterprise, honored the talent and humanity that Stewart brought to the role of Picard. "Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him," Shatner wrote on Instagram . "I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work." Patrick Stewart poses in his dressing room at the Lyceum Theater in New York in 2008 during a production of "Macbeth." AP Photo/Rick Maiman Stewart had a son, Daniel, and daughter, Sophie, with his first wife, Sheila Falconer, who he married in 1966. They divorced in 1990. In his 2023 memoir, Making It So , Stewart revealed that he had an affair with his Star Trek: The Next Generation costar Jennifer Hetrick during his marriage to Falconer, which led to their divorce and his estrangement from their children. "We don't have relationships," Stewart told the Irish Independent during his book tour. "I never thought that this would happen, but both my children are in their 50s — they're not children anymore, they're adults. And my relationship with them is practically non-existent." Stewart and Hetrick dated and were later engaged, but never married. In 2000, he married Wendy Neuss, one of the show's producers. They divorced three years later, after Stewart had an affair with actress Lisa Dillon, his costar in a stage production of The Master Builder . At the time, Stewart was 62 and Dillon was 23. "And so, another divorce. I felt stupid and responsible," Stewart wrote in his memoir. "I had cheated on my wife with a younger woman — again." Patrick Stewart and his wife Sunny Ozell arrive at Vanity Fair's Oscar party in 2024. AP Photo/Evan Agostini In 2008, Stewart met singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell at a restaurant in Brooklyn, where she was working as a waitress. Stewart was performing in a sold-out production of Macbeth , and gave her his phone number so he could arrange tickets for her. "[I] said 'Call me, I can get a ticket.' And that's what we did. And she came backstage afterward and we had dinner and here we are," Stewart told People magazine . They were married in 2013 in Ozell's home state of Nevada. Stewart's longtime friend and X-Men costar Ian McKellen officiated the ceremony. articles.title: Netanyahu's bloc maintains lead in Israeli election but doesn't secure majority
articles.summary: The final vote count from Tuesday's parliamentary election showed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc maintained its lead, securing 53 seats in the next Knesset, but no coalition secured a 61-seat majority. The opposition bloc seeking to replace the premier won 48 seats, according to official Central Elections Committee figures released on Thursday after all votes had been counted. Despite some claims of electoral interference, Israel's Election Committee also says the Knesset elections were conducted lawfully, adding there is no basis for claims of systematic interference with the integrity of the vote. Maya Levin,jewel Samad/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: This combination of pictures created on Oct. 28, 2026, shows Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot (L) addressing supporters at a rally in Tel Aviv and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressing his supporters at an election night rally in Jerusalem. Israel awaits election results as exit polls suggest close race for Netanyahu The two coalitions led by Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot may need the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties to have any chance of a majority in the Knesset. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have previously ruled out forming a coalition with the Arab parties. In his post-election speech, Netanyahu suggested that any government that included Arab parties would "endanger Israel." Arab party leaders have indicated willingness to work with the anti-Netanyahu opposition. The Arab-led Joint List -- a collection of three parties which between them were on course to win 12 seats as of Wednesday -- said in a statement that they were ready for "political cooperation to oust the Netanyahu government." The path to building a majority for the Netanyahu bloc is slim because it cannot form a coalition with the Arab Israeli parties due to the likely possibility it would lose the settler parties. Eisenkot's opposition party, however, does have a path to a majority with the backing of the Arab Israeli parties. Ohad Zwigenberg/AP Photo - PHOTO: An Arab woman walks with a child next to a torn Likud party campaign ad featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump, in Jerusalem on Oct. 28, 2026. No clear winner yet after polls close in Israeli elections, exit polls indicate "The Joint List will work with all its strength to bring an end to Netanyahu's rule. We are ready for political cooperation to establish an alternative government, which will present a true alternative and commit itself to a true change of the current government's racist policy," it said in a statement. Mansour Abbas, the leader of the United Arab List -- also known as Ra'am -- which was projected to win seven seats, said he had been in touch with representatives of both the Netanyahu and Eisenkot coalitions. Opposition leaders condemned the prime minister's remarks, maintaining that the elections in Israel were free and fair and there was no evidence of election fraud. The Israeli police said they will investigate any credible allegations of wrongdoing. Jalaa Marey/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gestures to his supporters at the election night rally after the first exit polls were announced, in Jerusalem on Oct. 28, 2026. Dean Livne, the acting director general of the CEC said on Wednesday that there was "no basis for allegations of election theft," as reported by Israel's Kan radio station. Eisenkot, meanwhile, said on Wednesday night that he had undertaken "a long day of meetings, conversations, and preparations to realize the will of the voter." "We are focused on the heavy task entrusted to us -- bringing change to Israel," he wrote in a post to X. ABC News' Nasser Atta and Joe Simonetti contributed to this report. articles.title: Google parent company sheds $482 billion in market value, the biggest drop in its history
articles.summary: Alphabet ( GOOGL ) had its worst day ever on Thursday. The stock fell nearly 13% after its third quarter results , steeper than any session since it went public in 2004, including its drops of more than 10% in March 2020 and September 2008. Alphabet lost $482 billion in stock market value, the second-biggest one-day loss ever for a US-listed company, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Only Nvidia ( NVDA ) has lost more, about $593 billion on Jan. 27, 2025, the day China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors. Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance That blew past the $400 billion SpaceX ( SPCX ) lost on June 22, the previous No. 2. In dollars, it was Alphabet's worst day by far. Its previous worst was about $275 billion on July 23. It was also the stock's steepest drop after an earnings report since the company went public, according to Bespoke Investment Group . The previous low was a slide of nearly 10% in July 2008. Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance The quarter gave both sides plenty to argue over. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to about $31 billion, and the Gemini app passed 1 billion users. But search revenue grew 12% to about $63 billion, short of Wall Street's roughly $65 billion estimate. Free cash flow — the cash left after paying for things like data centers — swung to a loss of about $9 billion as AI spending climbed. The company's stakes in AI labs cost it too. "The bears will argue this is the first quarter that AI is starting to seriously hurt their search business," Pivotal Research CEO Jeffrey Wlodarczak said in a rundown of why investors hated the quarter . CFRA's Angelo Zino was more patient, telling Yahoo Finance the pullback "probably represents a buying opportunity." Losses this size used to be unheard of. US-listed stocks have shed $200 billion or more in a single session 18 times this year through Wednesday. That's up from 13 in all of 2025 and none before 2022, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bloomberg data. Alphabet alone has lost about $1.4 trillion since its record in May. Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance Amazon ( AMZN ), the last of the big three cloud providers to report this week, posted faster growth and a record cash burn after Thursday's close. Amazon Web Services grew 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, while its 12-month free cash flow sank to a record outflow of more than $42 billion. Its stock fell after hours, a sign the pressure on AI spenders reaches well beyond Google. Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication. Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. articles.title: Trump administration renews bid to block 20,000 California ballots after court rebuke
articles.summary: An election worker places a ballot into a ballot box in Boyle Heights on Oct. 27, 2026. (Ronaldo Bolaños / Los Angeles Times) Soon after a federal judge in Los Angeles sharply rejected a Trump administration effort to block 20,000 California ballots from voters it alleged may be noncitizens, the U.S. Justice Department appealed — leaving attorneys on both sides preparing Thursday for yet another court battle. That was despite the lower court judge calling the request an unlawful threat to eligible voters in Tuesday’s midterm election and to free and fair American elections moving forward, and the same appellate court having already rejected the plan days  before. “Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” wrote First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the lead prosecutor in L.A. Early Thursday, Gov. Gavin Newsom swiped back at the Trump administration, writing, “A warning to Donald Trump: I’m deploying election lawyers to key battleground districts in California to protect every vote. And I just made it a FELONY to illegally seize ballots.” With just days to go until polls close, the heated election war between California and the Trump administration is showing no signs of slowing down despite multiple court orders rejecting the administration’s central effort to interfere in the midterms by accusing state and county officials of willfully turning a blind eye to voter fraud. That’s in part because lawyers within the U.S. Justice Department have been unrelenting in their pursuit of such control, both through court orders and threats to state and county officials — including through criminal grand jury subpoenas issued to at least three officials in Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan’s office. The subpoenas, reviewed by The Times, demand that the officials appear before prosecutors the day after the election with a slew of internal documents and testify as to how their office handled the Justice Department’s demands to set aside the ballots. It’s also because those same state and county officials have refused to yield, denouncing the threats  as unconvincing and illegal in recent letters back to the Justice Department. “Be aware that we consider DOJ’s efforts to threaten California election officials with criminal sanctions for following federal and state law to be an effort to unlawfully intimidate both election officials and California voters, which can undermine voters’ faith in the election process,” Susan K. Blitch, counsel for Monterey County, wrote in one. Read more: Judge denies feds' request to block 20,000 California ballots in blistering opinion Several election experts warned that Trump administration officials are trying to sow confusion and suspicion about an election in which the Republican Party is poised to lose ground, in part so they can reject the outcome. But they also said the courts have consistently rebuffed the Trump administration and will continue to do so through Nov. 3 and after — with the recent rulings over the 20,000 flagged ballots a perfect example. “The federal government lost in every way it could possibly lose. It lost on the law, and it lost on the facts, and it lost on the equities — [or] weighing the harms to the various parties,” said Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA School of Law. Appeal, rebuke, appeal Last week, Trump administration attorneys decided that U.S. District Judge David O. Carter was not ruling quickly enough on their emergency request for a temporary restraining order to block California, Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Logan from counting the 20,000 ballots the administration asserted were from “likely noncitizens” — so they appealed to the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals . On Monday, a three-judge panel there — including two appointees of President Trump and one of President Biden — denied the appeal for a lack of jurisdiction, because Carter hadn’t weighed in yet. However, two of the judges — Mark J. Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Gabriel P. Sanchez, the Biden appointee — wrote separately to make clear that they also would have denied the administration’s request for being likely unconstitutional and in violation of federal law. On Wednesday, Carter, an appointee of President Clinton, ruled that the administration’s allegations about noncitizen voters were “not credible” and that the intervention it sought would violate a host of federal laws, sow chaos in the ongoing midterm election, likely lead to the disenfranchisement of legitimate voters and foster future political meddling in elections. “This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote. “If [the Trump administration’s] last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.” Carter wrote that never in American history “has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.” The ruling — forceful, unequivocal and based on several of the same arguments made by Bennett and Sanchez — was cheered by state officials and voting rights groups. Election experts said it squared directly with their understanding of the law and was appropriate in the face of the Trump administration’s unprecedented, legally baseless effort to intervene in an ongoing state-run election. Justice Department lawyers filed a sparse appeal back to the 9th Circuit on Thursday, arguing the ongoing counting of ballots constitutes an emergency the court must intervene to stop, and asking it to do so by Friday. The same panel that previously rejected the request took the case back up, and gave the state, L.A. County and several voting rights groups until Friday morning to respond. War of words On Wednesday night, Newsom appeared on “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” and predicted Trump will take sweeping steps to “literally suppress the vote, to set the conditions where he will then express doubt in the electoral outcome, and suggest that it was rigged.” But he also said California is fighting back and prepared. “Right now, I am focused on getting over 1,000 poll workers, folks out there to monitor the DOJ monitors that Trump’s gonna send to try to steal this election,” Newsom said. “We have been running tabletop exercises. We have 1,000 volunteers. We have 134 election law attorneys that we’re sending out.” On Thursday, Essayli replied to the latter deployment, writing, “You’re going to protect every legal or illegal vote? What about California citizens whose votes are being diluted by ineligible voters. Do their constitutional rights matter.” Read more: Your last-minute voter guide to California's 2026 general election Trump, meanwhile, asserted with no evidence that “there are hundreds of thousands of bad ballots, bad votes, in California. Millions, in my opinion.” He said that California has “very corrupt elections,” and that if it had honest ones, he “would have won it by a lot.” The remarks were just the latest in a swirling and highly public war of words between state and federal officials. Federal prosecutors have issued three grand jury subpoenas to officials in Logan’s office. One dated Saturday and addressed to the office’s records custodian seeks internal emails, text messages, guidance and discussions related to the Trump administration’s demands that Logan’s office investigate alleged noncitizen voters. It orders the custodian to appear in Santa Ana on Wednesday, the day after the election, or provide the records and a signed certification beforehand. Prosecutors are also seeking records describing how the county screens for unlawful voting, prevents noncitizen ballots from being counted and handles evidence that noncitizens voted in federal elections or that others helped them to do so. A Justice Department spokesperson said it doesn’t comment on grand jury subpoenas, but noted Carter had “explained that voting unlawfully results in criminal exposure.” Carter did say that a “clear remedy” to the administration’s concerns already existed, in that prosecutors could criminally charge individuals committing voter fraud. But he also explicitly denounced what he called the administration’s “threat” to charge election officials, writing that “these threats must stop.” Logan, in a statement, said Carter’s “admonishment about threats directed at election officials on Tuesday was well placed and appreciated. At every step, the U.S. Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach. Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law.” In Carter’s courtroom Tuesday , Essayli claimed the federal government has maintained a collaborative “tone” since it first demanded the state set aside ballots, and said he was surprised at how “adversarial” state election officials had been. But Essayli and other Justice Department officials have been engaged for weeks in an aggressive back and forth with California officials online — which is highly unusual for prosecutors actively litigating related cases. When Newsom’s office recently wrote that “Trump’s DOJ is so desperate to invent ‘widespread voter fraud,’ it sent California counties lists of people who NEVER voted — and voters from the WRONG COUNTY. Absolute clown show!” Essayli shot back, “Hey Fraud King,” with a crown emoji. “We’re not waiting for them to vote.” Also unusual have been the threats Justice Department attorneys have been sending to county election officials in California, including in a series of letters Friday in which they asserted varying numbers of “likely aliens” per county, set a 48-hour deadline for the counties to cooperate with federal authorities to prove those voters are citizens. In one letter to Kristin Connelly, head of the Contra Costa County registrar’s office, U.S. Atty. Craig Missakian flagged 407 potential noncitizens in the county and said he was writing “to make unmistakably clear the legal implications” of processing any ballots from those voters. On Wednesday, Thomas L. Geiger, Contra Costa County counsel, responded with his own letter, questioning the accuracy of the noncitizen claims and saying it would be “legally unsound” for Connelly to “disregard both California and federal law” in order to comply with Missakian’s demands. Other California officials have signaled a willingness to work with federal authorities. San Luis Obispo County District Atty. Dan Dow said Thursday that his office is investigating “63 federally identified suspect registrations” off a list also provided to the county clerk-recorder. Get the L.A. articles.title: DOJ reportedly issues new wave of subpoenas in criminal probe of Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: It was, for a while, considered one of those colorful quirks that crop up in the course of an election: the fact that not one but two candidates named Dan Sullivan will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot for U.S. senator from Alaska. One Dan Sullivan — Dan S. Sullivan — is the state's incumbent Republican senator. He is trying to fend off a fierce challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and secure a third term. The other Dan Sullivan — Dan J. Sullivan — is a retired teacher from a tiny fishing village along the Alaska Panhandle. He has never previously campaigned for public office, and he switched his registration from "unaffiliated" to "Republican " just before the deadline to run. (He has since switched back to unaffiliated .) But now the situation seems to be getting more serious. At President Trump's direction, the Justice Department last week sued in federal court to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant whose purpose is to siphon away votes. Then, on Wednesday, the New York Times published an extensive investigation that appears to substantiate that allegation , calling it "Democrats' secret effort to stack Alaska's ballot." "The Times has found, based on interviews and text messages, along with documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign, that not only did Ms. Peltola's team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader," the paper wrote. "The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent's support and help catapult the Democrat to victory." Matthew Salisbury, a former congressional candidate and Alaska insurance manager, told the Times that he was approached by a man claiming to represent wealthy donors who wanted him to run for Senate as an independent candidate. Salisbury said he met with the man over beers at an Irish pub in Anchorage, but ultimately declined after being unable to verify his identity. "I'm not naïve," he said. In response to the report, Trump called for both Peltola and the "fake" Dan Sullivan to be removed from the ballot in a post on Truth Social . Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was ordering an investigation to determine whether the alleged effort violated state law. "Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support," Dunleavy said in a statement . "Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections." Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a Republican who has represented Alaska in the Senate since 2022, wrote in a statement that the people of her state deserve a full explanation. "Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments," she wrote. "By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong." Sam Curtis, a spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Law, told CNN that the revelations in the Times report did not change the state's opposition to a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to potentially delay certification of the election. "Placing candidates on the ballot is a matter of state law, not federal law," Curtis said, adding that the report has "no impact on the current litigation." Rep. James Comer, the Republican head of the House Oversight Committee, said Thursday that the committee is "taking action" to launch an investigation into the matter, including an inquiry into whether any crimes may have been committed. ABC News also reported Thursday that the DOJ had issued a wave of new subpoenas as it probes whether the alleged recruitment scheme may have run afoul of federal conspiracy laws. Yahoo The outcome of the legal dispute, if it moves forward, could have enormous national implications. Democrats need to win at least a few Senate races in historically Republican states to secure a majority in the chamber. Polls suggest Alaska is one of their best chances to turn a red seat blue. Given how close other races across the country appear to be, a legal ruling that erases a narrow Peltola victory could be the pivot point that allows the GOP to keep control of the Senate for the last two years of Trump's presidency. How did this happen, and where do things go from here? Here's everything you need to know to catch up and make sense of the story. How Alaska wound up with two Dan Sullivans on the ballot Ballot-stacking — the process of recruiting a spoiler candidate to help your candidate win — isn't unheard of in politics, and the Times says it's "generally considered legal." But it's a lot easier in Alaska than other states because of the unique way elections work there. When Peltola ran for reelection to the U.S. House in 2024, the state GOP backed an effort to help a second Democrat — an inmate who conducted his campaign from a New York prison — remain on the ballot. And during this year's primaries, super PACs aligned with both parties "flooded the state with ads for fringe candidates" in an attempt to "dilute support for the mainstream candidates opposed by the groups," according to an October Alaska Beacon report . How is any of this possible? The Last Frontier sends the top four primary candidates to the general election regardless of party — then asks voters to rank them on Election Day in order of preference. This means that candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves. (Dan J. Sullivan initially claimed to be a Republican .) It also means that as long as they finish in the top four, primary candidates don't have to earn many votes to secure their very own ballot line on Nov. 3. (Dan J. Sullivan won 4,107 ). For months, Republicans have questioned Dan J. Sullivan's intentions and tried to get him tossed off the ballot. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court dismissed their arguments, ruling that neither state law nor the U.S. Constitution provided any legal basis for removing Dan J. Sullivan's name. How the Senate candidates will appear on Alaska's midterm ballot. elections.alaska.gov The more obscure Sullivan has "maintained that he [is] running in good faith and of his own volition, as a moderate Republican and not a secret Democrat," as a Times profile put it in August. He said he'd voted in the past for some Alaska Republicans, including Sen. Lisa Murkowski, even though he also "acknowledged previous donations to Ms. Peltola and a handful of other Democrats," and said he would prefer Peltola for Senate over the Republican incumbent "if it was between those two." But according to this week's Times report, "operatives aligned with" the Peltola campaign convinced Dan J. Sullivan to enter the race "to help Mary." The report cited as its sources 12 people "who participated in or were told of the plan" as well as interviews with other would-be recruits and dozens of internal text messages. For the record, both Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which directs the party's campaign strategy in Senate races across the country, have denied any "involvement," and Dan J. Sullivan did not respond to the Times's repeated requests for comment. One of the Times's main sources — former Peltola campaign manager and longtime aide Elisa Rios, who had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit — also tried to retract her statements to the paper ahead of publication. The Times story described an elaborate endeavor — which was "internally called the ballot composition project" — that "involved secret trips to far-flung Alaskan communities and the appearance of a mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs." The Times also reported that the "Peltola campaign's lawyers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee" were "involved" with the effort. The Trump administration's lawsuit Legal battles over the dual Dan Sullivan issue had been confined to state courts until last week. That's when Trump's administration filed its lawsuit aiming to have the certification of the results blocked if Peltola wins a close election that may have been affected by Dan J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot. "Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election," the Department of Justice wrote in its legal filing. "I'm the one that said do it," Trump said Friday of the lawsuit . The suit argues that a Democratic victory should be considered invalid if Peltola wins by a margin smaller than the total number of votes that Dan J. Sullivan receives — under the assumption that those votes may have come from confused voters who intended to vote for the incumbent Republican senator instead. Democrats have asked the courts to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the administration lacks "any statutory or constitutional authority to insert itself" into the state's electoral process. Alaska's state government, which is currently led by Republicans, has also filed to dismiss the administration's lawsuit. On Monday, a federal judge agreed to fast-track consideration of the dispute to potentially allow it to be resolved before Election Day. Many legal experts say the lawsuit has a slim chance of success. First, it requires a very specific outcome in which Peltola wins by what would likely need to be a very thin margin. Even in that scenario, election law experts say, the appearance of confusion on the part of voters does not create legal grounds for the federal DOJ to have the results rejected. "I believe that this lawsuit is abusive in its intentions and borders on frivolous in its arguments, and that it is destined for defeat in the courts should it reach the merits," Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, told the Alaska Beacon . Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a Harvard law professor, told the Harvard Gazette that the law the administration is relying on in its lawsuit — the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — does not give federal authorities any power to challenge state election procedures. "The lawsuit has nothing to do with voter registration. There's no allegation that anybody is improperly registered in Alaska; there's no claim that Alaska isn't in compliance with the NVRA's requirements for voter registration," Stephanopoulos said. More generally, experts say the lawsuit runs against the Constitution's language granting states the power to run their own elections. "This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," David Becker, a former Justice Department attorney who worked on voting rights cases, told Alaska Public Media . What's next? The federal judge in Alaska considering Democrats' motion to dismiss the lawsuit i ssued an order late Wednesday allowing their challenge to move forward. She gave the DOJ until Thursday afternoon to respond. That likely only matters in an extremely close race, which is not the recent norm in Alaska. The last time Dan S. Sullivan was on the ballot, he defeated his top challenger, independent candidate Al Gross, by 45,000 votes . The most recent Senate race, in 2022, was closer, but the top two finishers were both Republicans. Things are expected to be much tighter this time around. Peltola has held a consistent lead in the polls since the summer, but her advantage has steadily shrunk in the months leading up to Election Day. The most recent surveys have her ahead by 2 points, well within the margin for Sullivan to win. The Cook Political Report, one of the nation's most respected election forecasters, lists the race as a toss-up. Another well-regarded forecaster, the Center for Politics, categorizes it as "leans Democrat." articles.title: Pentagon accuses fired 3-star general of leaking classified information
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Pentagon has accused a newly ousted three-star general of leaking sensitive information to the media just hours after officials confirmed his removal from a top military planning post. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia as head of strategy, plans and policy for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, a defense official said late Wednesday. Typically, the general in the position and their staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans for both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the president. No reason was given for the firing, the latest in a series of ousters or departures of military leaders under Hegseth. However, a Pentagon official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, later said in a statement that Sylvia was under investigation over allegations of sharing classified information about the Iran war , the Russia-Ukraine conflict and other topics with journalists. The statement claims that Sylvia failed three polygraph tests about leaking classified information. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a social media post that the department “took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information” without mentioning Sylvia by name. He said the matter has been sent to the Justice Department for "potential further legal action." It is not clear why the Pentagon would appear to be pursuing charges in civilian courts instead of trying the general in the military justice system. Sylvia did not immediately respond to a voicemail, text messages, emails and a LinkedIn message on accounts and numbers that appear to belong to him. When asked about Sylvia’s firing by reporters Thursday, President Donald Trump said, "She’s gonna have big problems,” incorrectly identifying the male general as a woman. “We’re very much looking for leakers,” Trump said. In a confusing twist, the Joint Staff on Thursday also withdrew a statement from a day earlier that wished Sylvia well because “upon further review, we determined that the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances.” A spokesperson late Wednesday had said the Joint Staff extended its “deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation.” The firing of Sylvia from the Pentagon's top military planning post comes as Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran in the eight-month-long war following next week's midterm elections. The Pentagon official, however, insisted Sylvia was not a “central planner” on the Iran conflict and said that was the purview of U.S. Central Command. Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the office he recently led. His military awards include six Bronze Star Medals, including one for valor, and a Purple Heart, indicating he was wounded in combat. Sylvia's case is Hegseth's latest accusation against top Pentagon officials of leaking to the media. He fired three aides from his inner circle last year as part of a broader leak investigation that included polygraph tests. In a joint statement shared by senior aide Dan Caldwell , the trio protested the firing and said they were “incredibly disappointed by the manner in which our service at the Department of Defense ended. Unnamed Pentagon officials have slandered our character with baseless attacks on our way out the door.” Hegseth never provided more information on what the three were accused of, and Caldwell would go on to be hired by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. Under Hegseth, the Pentagon also has carried out a series of moves restricting media access , including requiring that journalists be escorted while on Pentagon grounds and declaring that its press office was a classified space inaccessible to journalists. ___ Associated Press writer Seung Min Kim contributed to this report. articles.title: Hegseth's treatment of lawmakers threatens Trump's $1.5 trillion defense plan
articles.summary: This summer, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asked a Republican lawmaker what he thought the odds were that Congress would pass the Trump administration’s record $1.5 trillion defense budget request. The chances, the lawmaker responded, were about the same as Hegseth getting confirmed again by the Senate. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. “You have a problem, and you need to increase the amount and the quality of the communication” with Congress, the Republican lawmaker recounted in an interview, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe the private exchange. Months later, members of both parties said the Pentagon has not changed course. For decades, defense issues have mostly remained insulated from Washington’s toxic partisanship. But Republicans and Democrats say they increasingly fear that fire wall no longer exists. With just over 20 legislative days left in the year - and next week’s election likely to empower Democrats eager to confront Hegseth - lawmakers are deadlocked on their major defense policy and spending bills. Failure would leave the Pentagon with few options to replace the thousands of weapons spent during eight months of war with Iran and halt the administration’s ambitious military agenda. To understand how the consensus collapsed, The Washington Post spoke with 30 people at the center of national security in Congress, including 20 lawmakers who sit on the committees that oversee the Pentagon and its budget. Republicans argued that Democrats are stalling critical military funding to placate voters incensed at President Donald Trump. Democrats framed their opposition as a necessary check on an administration that the GOP-controlled House and Senate have refused to hold accountable for starting a war without the approval of Congress. But most lawmakers who spoke with The Post described the impasse in more personal terms. Hegseth’s adversarial behavior - from withholding information to attacking Democrats and some Republicans - was straining the bipartisan dealmaking that has long ensured support for the military, members of both parties said. “The people who have been around for a few days have seen what normal looks like,” Rep. Joe Courtney (D-Connecticut) said. “We’re not living in normal.” In a statement, Pentagon spokesman Joel Valdez defended Hegseth’s approach, saying the secretary is “always willing to engage directly with any lawmakers who bring forward their concerns in good faith.” “Lawmakers understand exactly how critical the National Defense Authorization Act and defense appropriations are to military readiness,” Valdez said, referring to the pending bills. “We do not expect them to deliberately cripple the force or our warfighting capability simply to score political points.” The collapse of bipartisanship The NDAA is widely considered a must-pass bill. The legislation, which covers issues from troop pay to weapons production, has advanced for 65 consecutive years. A similar, albeit less reliable, coalition helps pass the annual defense spending bill, which provides the money to pay troops, buy weapons and conduct military operations worldwide. The group of Republicans and Democrats who typically support the legislation has fractured this year. The NDAA failed to advance in the Senate and barely passed the House, where more Republicans voted against it than Democrats voted for it. The two chambers are negotiating a final version with votes expected later this fall. At greater risk of failing, most lawmakers said, is the annual defense budget. The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion plan would fund a range of advanced weaponry, from commercial-style drones to precision missiles depleted during the Iran war. It would direct billions more toward some of Trump’s personal projects for the military, including a Golden Dome missile defense shield, a fleet of battleships named after him and a renaming of the Defense Department as the “War Department.” Hegseth has called the 40 percent increase in spending an “urgent, necessary injection of resources” to outpace America’s adversaries. He has also urged Congress to approve an additional $67 billion in funding to help cover the costs of the Iran war and other military operations around the world. Nearly all Senate Democrats blocked the request in an extraordinary act of protesting the conflict. In a move that has frustrated some Republicans, the administration split the defense budget into two buckets: $1.15 trillion that will require some Democratic support and another $350 billion meant to pass with GOP votes alone. Republicans have so far failed to agree on a strategy to pass the party-line share of funding. The gridlock has left the military vulnerable, lawmakers said. U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, estimated that as of mid-October the Iran conflict had cost more than $47 billion, forcing the Pentagon to delay trainings and maintenance projects just to cover its bills. After failing to reach a lasting ceasefire this summer, the president has threatened to restart strikes after the midterms. “Russia and China are questioning whether or not we have the resources and the ability to quickly replace dwindling stocks and ammunition,” said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota), who faulted Democrats for holding up the defense budget. “You’re mad at the president, but you’re taking it out on these men and women who are following orders.” Excluding the Democrats Democrats say the Trump administration is blaming them for problems of its own making. “To come in and say, ‘Oh, by the way, we made this choice and we spent all this money and we need you to replenish it’ - it takes a lot of nerve,” said Sen. Angus King (Maine), an independent who caucuses with Democrats. The Trump administration has excluded Democrats from several briefings on the $350 billion in defense spending it hopes to pass on a party-line vote. These meetings have broken a long-standing practice of sharing national security information equally with each party, lawmakers said. Multiple Republicans noted that the administration has tightened the briefings in part because of concerns about leaks to the news media, which Trump officials have blamed on congressional Democrats. Many in the GOP said they had urged the Pentagon to include both parties. “If we are asking them to make these country-altering decisions, I think we have to inform them,” said Sen. Kevin Cramer (North Dakota), one of multiple Republicans who noted they’d urged the Pentagon to share more information with Democrats. The Republican lawmaker who offered Hegseth his blunt assessment of the $1.5 trillion request also said that Democrats are partly to blame for the lack of communication. Earlier this year, the lawmaker said, he brokered a private meeting between Hegseth and a small group of Democrats. All of the Democrats declined to meet with the secretary, the lawmaker said. Other members of Congress faulted Hegseth for the distrust. In April, while appearing before the House Armed Services Committee, Hegseth delivered a broadside in his opening remarks. “The biggest adversary we face at this point,” he said, “are the reckless, feckless and defeatist words of congressional Democrats and some Republicans.” At one point during the hearing, Rep. Austin Scott (Georgia), a senior Republican on the committee, noted that the administration would need Republican and Democratic votes to secure its budget. “The way Hegseth treats people is a problem,” Scott said in an interview. ‘Shockingly unprofessional’ During Hegseth’s first private meeting with the Senate Armed Services Committee, in June 2025, he opened with a warning, according to three people familiar with his remarks. Though the hearing was classified, the secretary said, he didn’t know - and didn’t trust - everyone in the room and would watch what he said, these people recalled. They cited the exchange as an example of Hegseth’s combativeness. “It’s as shockingly unprofessional as anything I see,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who voted against Hegseth’s confirmation and has opposed the Iran war, said of the secretary’s tone. Current and former officials familiar with Hegseth’s relationships on Capitol Hill disputed assertions that the Pentagon was withholding information from Congress or refusing to meet with Democrats. They said Hegseth’s private meetings had been professional and noted that Democrats had openly attacked him, accusing him of mismanagement and dishonesty. The Pentagon did not directly address questions about this encounter or others detailed in this report. The contentious relationship has led some Republicans to ask the Pentagon to instead send uniformed officers to brief Congress, lawmakers said. Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has hosted private breakfasts with Republicans and Democrats at the Pentagon in an attempt to build more bipartisan support for the budget, according to lawmakers and others familiar with the sessions. A spokesperson for Caine declined to comment. Meanwhile, members of both parties voiced a sense of resignation that the defense-related committees were becoming more partisan. “Democrats don’t want to work on anything in a bipartisan way that could be construed as giving Trump a win,” said Sen. Deb Fischer (Nebraska), a senior Republican. Many Democrats said they are worried that the Pentagon’s shortfalls could hamstring military readiness for years, including in a future Democratic administration. But they argued that they need to use every tool they have to resist what they see as an unconstitutional war. “We are taking serious risks with our national security and should not be,” said Sen. Chris Coons (Delaware), the top Democrat on the Senate panel on defense spending. “At the end of the day, the president’s responsible for the decisions he’s made.” Multiple people familiar with the budget negotiations, some speaking on the condition of anonymity to provide their candid assessment, said that the Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion request was probably impossible with so little time left in the year. A U.S. official familiar with Hegseth’s relationships with lawmakers asserted that the full budget request was still viable and that Republicans, if they lose control of Congress, would see this as their last chance to secure defense-related priorities without Democratic votes. Doubts about the budget have come at a low point for Hegseth’s standing with congressional Republicans, who have signaled they will oppose his preferred picks to lead the Army and criticized him more openly in recent weeks. When the House returns in November, Hegseth will probably face an impeachment vote, led by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky), over the Iran war. Meanwhile, some Democrats felt emboldened heading into next week’s election - they appear likely to at least regain control of the House - and the prospect of launching aggressive oversight of the Pentagon. Earlier this year, Hegseth held private breakfasts with the top Republicans and Democrats on the Armed Services committees, in an effort to improve his standing. Rep. Adam Smith (Washington), the House Armed Services Committee’s top Democrat, recalled saying near the end of his meeting with Hegseth that, despite their disagreements, they didn’t have to be enemies. In an interview, Smith said he wasn’t looking to partner with “this Pentagon.” “I’m looking,” he added, “for ways to stop the awful things they’re doing with our military.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/10/29/inside-breakdown-trumps-15-trillion-pentagon-plan/

articles.title: Obama-era investigation found evidence against Ilhan Omar's marriage, report says
articles.summary: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images) Federal investigators found evidence during the Obama administration suggesting that Rep. Ilhan Omar's 2009 marriage to a man suspected of being her brother was intended to help him obtain a green card, but the case stalled chiefly because prosecutors concluded the suspected offense fell outside a five-year statute of limitations, according to a new report. The FBI and Department of Homeland Security investigated the marriage in the summer of 2016, current and former officials told The New York Times in a report published Thursday. The officials' account challenges Omar's characterization of the earlier inquiry as having debunked allegations that she married her brother to help him obtain a green card. The newspaper said it remains unclear what evidence investigators had establishing that Omar and her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, are siblings. Marrying a person to help them obtain a green card is illegal under federal law, while marrying a sibling is illegal under state law. However, the newspaper noted that it remains unclear whether federal prosecutors could pursue charges against Omar despite the statute of limitations for marriage-based immigration fraud. Omar has repeatedly denied the allegations about her and her ex-husband. "Rep. Omar has repeatedly and unequivocally denied this baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory," spokeswoman Jackie Rogers said in a statement. "This is a desperate political smear designed to distract from Trump's failed presidency and two years of Republican failure in Congress." Six current and former officials familiar with the 2016 investigation told the Times that agents found evidence suggesting Omar and Elmi were siblings. The officials said investigators had limited tools to develop the case because prosecutors did not pursue it. Omar was already a U.S. citizen when she married Elmi, a British citizen, in 2009. They divorced in 2017. Two former officials said Elmi obtained a conditional two-year green card through the marriage. When immigration authorities requested additional evidence before granting him permanent status without conditions, he left the United States and abandoned his petition, they said. The earlier inquiry involved an FBI agent specializing in public corruption and civil rights cases and two Homeland Security Investigations agents, according to the report. The allegations surfaced publicly in 2016 as Omar campaigned for a seat in the Minnesota House of Representatives. After a local television station reported that the U.S. attorney's office had opened an investigation, her campaign sought a letter from Andrew Luger, then the U.S. attorney for Minnesota. In the Aug. 22, 2016, letter, Luger wrote that "my office is not investigating, nor have we requested an investigation into Ms. Omar." Omar portrayed the letter as an exoneration that put to rest "flat-out falsehoods." Luger, however, told the Times last week that the letter "was never meant to say anything about the substance of the claims." He said it was intended only to rebut an erroneous report that he had asked ICE to investigate Omar. Luger said federal agents could have been pursuing the matter without his knowledge and denied shielding Omar from scrutiny. The Trump administration has reopened scrutiny of the marriage as part of a broader investigation into the Omar family's immigration history. Federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington home Oct. 12, weeks before she seeks a fifth term in the House. Investigators are also examining whether Omar's late father submitted false or incomplete information during the immigration process and whether Omar was too old to qualify for citizenship through him in 2000, the Times reported. Democrats have condemned the inquiry as political persecution and said the search violated Justice Department policy intended to prevent investigative actions from influencing elections. President Donald Trump repeated the allegation that Omar married her brother last week. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the broader investigation could lead to Omar's deportation if authorities establish that she should not have been admitted to the country. © 2026 Newsmax. articles.title: Speaker Johnson signals he will keep leading Republicans even if they lose the House
articles.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) recent hints that he intends to remain GOP leader even if Republicans lose the House have rattled the party’s leadership outlook and raised fresh new questions about the GOP’s future heading into the next Congress. Most House Speakers in recent decades have stepped out of Congress after losing the gavel. And Reps. Steve Scalise (R-La.), the majority leader, and Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), a conservative icon, are both expected to launch bids to lead House Republicans if Democrats flip the chamber, according to GOP lawmakers, aides and strategists. But Johnson recently muddled the leadership landscape by signaling his intention to keep his spot atop the party even if Republicans are knocked out of power. Then on Monday, President Trump offered a glowing endorsement of Johnson’s leadership chops, sparking further speculation that Johnson might, in fact, buck historic trends and try to remain leader even from the minority. “Mike Johnson is a true friend, fighter, and WINNER,” Trump posted on social media, “and he has my Complete and Total endorsement for Re-Election.” “Thank you, President @realDonaldTrump!” Johnson responded. “The best is yet to come as we save America!” Much about the leadership race is expected to come into sharper focus after next Tuesday’s midterm elections. A Johnson spokesperson said the Speaker is “solely focused on protecting the majority,” noting that he “will campaign in 21 districts across 13 states between now and Election Day.” But many Republicans are skeptical, predicting Johnson will follow the example of past GOP Speakers — including Newt Gingrich (Ga.), Dennis Hastert (Ill.), Paul Ryan (Wis.) and Kevin McCarthy (Calif.) — who all left Capitol Hill in short order after losing the gavel. “I highly doubt that the Speaker will go for minority leader at this point,” a GOP aide said Wednesday. “I just don't see him having a desire. I don't think he's having a fun time as Speaker. I don't think he'd want to be minority leader.” Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) defied modern tradition in 2011, when she clung to the minority leader seat after the party was clobbered in the 2010 midterms. Pelosi would win the gavel back eight years later, but she’s been the exception. GOP strategist Amy Frederiksen said, “When you lose, and you're no longer Speaker …it's hard to go back to minority leader.” “There’s certainly a lot less trappings and a lot less power, and also the caucus just tends to kind of want to clean some house. Like members just see it as an opportunity to just switch things up, and so it's not that it hasn't happened, of course. Speaker Pelosi went to be the minority leader, so it isn't unprecedented,” Frederiksen said. “It wouldn't be historic in any kind of way, and it's very possible. But it is — I don't think it's as simple as him just deciding. I think that the caucus is going to really want to weigh in on things.” She added that Johnson was a “compromise candidate anyway” for Speaker. “We went through a couple, two, three, four different potential Speakers, including Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan, when he was finally chosen as Speaker, so I, you know, I just think that there is that,” she said. “It was sort of a bargain struck anyway for him to be Speaker.” Some Republicans predicted next year’s leadership roster will hinge on how the midterms play out. Although Trump is not on the ballot, the elections are shaping up to be a referendum on the president, whose historic unpopularity has created huge challenges for GOP candidates and made Democrats the favorite to control the House next year. Still, some Republicans believe that if Democrats win by a wide margin, Johnson will bear much of the blame, lose support within the conference and struggle to secure the votes needed to become minority leader, even if Trump wanted him there. “I would imagine there to be more of a push for someone else, just given that over, you know, a billion dollars has been spent on the midterms alone,” a second GOP staffer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The Hill earlier this month. Although both Scalise and Jordan have downplayed their interest in the top spot, many Republicans say they’re both angling for the position, setting the stage for a potentially messy internal fight when House lawmakers return to Washington the week after the midterms. (Minnesota Rep. Tom Emmer, the Republican whip, says he wants to remain in that seat). There’s plenty of disagreement about who would have the advantage in such a race. Some say that if it’s a two-way race between Scalise and Jordan, Scalise would likely be better positioned than Jordan to step into the top spot given his current leadership position. “I think for Scalise … it'd be an easy transition for him to step into that. But for Jordan, he's really — how do I phrase this? He's been a loyal soldier. He's rallied people well, and he's an effective politician. So I think both would do well in the role, but I think Scalise would have an easier transition just out of pure — his House leadership currently,” a third GOP staffer said. The first Republican staffer, though, predicted Jordan has the edge. “He's done a lot of work over the past couple years where he's kind of built his own coalition, [and] he does have, like, a cult following around the country when he goes on the campaign trail. So I do think it's his to lose at this point,” the first aide said. “When you're in the minority, you need somebody who can be a fighter and willing to go out there and go on TV and bomb some bombs. And I think he's the guy for it.” The offices of Scalise and Jordan did not respond to requests for comment on Wednesday. Johnson has faced a rocky tenure as Speaker, often marked by internal GOP fighting, a razor-thin margin and repeated challenges in keeping his conference united on government spending, the Iran war and other issues. Even so, Johnson told CBS News’s Robert Costa this month that in the “unlikely scenario” Republicans lose the House, “I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government.” “I’m going to continue to serve my highest best use to God and country, and I believe right now, as we’re sitting here, that’s the Speaker of the House,” Johnson said. “And if we lost the majority, I don’t think that that position that I have would change. I think I would stay right there.” Some Republicans note that if Johnson were to jump into the minority leader race, he would have a strong case for the position. The third GOP staffer noted Johnson’s “had to deal with a lot of curveballs” and that he’s handled them well. “I think that the party recognizes that and will react accordingly,” the staffer said. “That doesn't mean there's not people gunning for the same spot, but I think Johnson has been a good leader, a team player amidst what is, you know — we could say honestly — has been some chaos at times.” Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. articles.title: 微软250亿美元债券发行获4.6倍认购，但30年期利差高于评级更低的宝洁，债市消化能力趋于极限
articles.summary: 微软以稀缺的AAA信用评级和亮眼的财报背书，成功完成一笔规模达250亿美元的债券发行，创下美国企业债市场历史上最受追捧的交易之一。然而，这场盛况背后，债券市场对AI超大规模云计算商（hyperscaler）的选择性分化已愈发清晰。 此次发行吸引高峰订单逾1150亿美元，认购倍数达4.6倍。承销团队由富国银行、摩根大通和瑞银领衔，并将最长期限债券的利差从初始指导价收窄最多30个基点。 微软首席财务官Amy Hood在本周业绩电话会议上表示，公司将在"认为时机合适时"进一步融资。 不过，市场人士警告， 微软的成功并不代表其他科技巨头同样将获得同等热情的接待。 近期围绕AI支出与盈利能力的隐忧已令高风险科技债承压——博通和SpaceX的信用违约互换成本一度触及历史高位。 Natixis Investment Managers Solutions多资产组合经理兼首席策略师Jack Janasiewicz表示，"信贷市场正在承担大量甄别赢家与输家的工作，市场对发行仍然开放，但并非对所有人都开放。" 周四微软收跌0.16%。 AAA评级优势：微软的稀缺身份 微软此番发行距其上一次叩响美国投资级债券市场已近八年——2017年曾融资170亿美元。 此次推出的10笔不同期限债券，涵盖2年至40年，其中40年期债券的定价利差约为基准国债上方105个基点，明显低于Alphabet同期限债券约133个基点的水平，后者评级亦低于微软。 在评级层面， 微软是美国上市公司中除强生外唯一同时获得穆迪和标普AAA顶级评级的企业， 这一身份赋予其在拥挤的科技债供给中脱颖而出的天然优势。 GW&K Investment Management组合经理Brett Kozlowski表示，"这笔交易的时机感觉颇具机会主义色彩"，强劲需求在意料之中，主要来自市场对"极为罕见的长久期AAA债券"的渴求，加之逾6%的收益率形成吸引力。 微软本周三公布的财季业绩亦为此次发行提供了有力支撑——云计算收入同比增长48%，资本支出亦维持在可控区间，缓解了投资者对AI大手笔投入的担忧。 CreditSights分析师在周四发布的报告中指出，250亿美元的债券发行将使微软的总租约调整后杠杆率仅微升至0.7倍，资产负债表依然健康。 债市消化能力趋于极限，微软30年期利差高于评级更低的宝洁 尽管微软此番顺风顺水，但整个超大规模云计算行业的债券供给已接近投资者所能承受的上限。 据彭博汇编数据，截至周四， 超大规模云计算商及数据中心开发商今年通过全球投资级债券发行已累计融资逾3130亿美元，较2025年全年规模高出近两倍， 并推动全球债券发行总量飙升至创纪录的6.63万亿美元。 面对市场饱和，部分大型借款方已开始主动降温。甲骨文本周披露，承诺至2030财年净债务增量上限为100亿美元，以缓解投资者对其债务扩张的担忧；Meta则转向股票市场，完成了250亿美元的股权融资。 微软自身的定价也折射出市场的审慎情绪。 尽管坐拥AAA评级，其30年期债券利差达基准国债上方95个基点，反而高于评级更低的宝洁公司同周发行的30年期债券——后者以60个基点的利差定价，创2003年以来最低溢价。 Wealth Enhancement董事兼高级投资策略师Ayako Yoshioka表示："对于5年、7年期的微软债券，我会毫不犹豫地认购。但一旦拉长到30年期，商业模式层面的不确定性仍然需要在定价中有所体现。" 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.summary: SpaceX的AI业务正以前所未有的速度改变这家火箭公司的营收结构，而这一转变背后，一家AI初创公司的押注举足轻重。 据彭博援引一位知情人士透露， AI公司Anthropic PBC是SpaceX目前最大的单一客户，在今年第三季度贡献了SpaceX逾三分之一的营收。 这一消息意味着，这家以火箭和卫星业务起家的公司，如今对单一AI计算客户的依赖程度已超过美国联邦政府。 SpaceX上周在一份文件中披露，第三季度约34.5%的营收来自旗下AI部门（现更名为Super Intelligence）的单一客户，该客户在文件中仅被标注为"客户B"。 上述知情人士确认，"客户B"即为Anthropic，但以信息属于私密为由拒绝具名。 这一敞口令市场对SpaceX的收入稳定性产生疑虑——Anthropic最早可在明年行使合同退出权。 SpaceX周四收跌0.92%。截至发稿，盘后进一步下跌1.7%。 AI算力业务首度盈利，营收结构深度重塑 Anthropic对SpaceX的付款源于双方今年早些时候签署的合同，Anthropic将使用SpaceX位于田纳西州孟菲斯数据中心的算力资源。 马斯克正逐步将SpaceX的AI业务打造为所谓的"新云"（neocloud）模式，向Anthropic及Alphabet旗下谷歌等客户出租数据中心算力。 这一押注在本季度初见成效：SpaceX的AI业务实现首次盈利，也为马斯克描绘的"2026年底实现年化营收1000亿美元"目标提供了支撑。 然而，AI算力业务的强劲表现同时令SpaceX高度依赖单一客户，而这恰恰发生在华尔街对neocloud行业信心趋于冷淡之际。 合同规模庞大，但退出条款埋下隐患 根据Anthropic的IPO披露文件，该公司已承诺在合同期内（至2029年）向SpaceX支付最高1205亿美元，相当于从今年12月起每月约31亿美元。 然而，合同中设有明确的退出窗口： Anthropic可分别在2027年1月和2027年3月之后提前90天通知终止合同。 此外，Anthropic还与Nscale、Lambda等其他neocloud供应商签有协议，进一步凸显其维持多元算力供应商策略的意图，也意味着SpaceX并非其唯一选择。 马斯克警示neocloud洗牌，但坚称SpaceX自身差异化 就在neocloud行业承压之际，马斯克近几周来在其社交平台X上频繁发声——X现已归属SpaceX旗下。他点评了CoreWeave高收益债券的处境，并着力强调SpaceX与其他neocloud竞争对手的不同之处。 "债务市场几乎已对任何缺乏AI数据中心以外实质性营收的公司关闭融资渠道，"马斯克表示，并指出SpaceX同时拥有Starlink和火箭发射业务作为营收支柱。 "这意味着200多家neocloud将迎来鱼苗级别的死亡与整合，部分能活下来，但不会太多。" 政府合同地位式微，NASA占比或跌破5% Anthropic营收占比超越美国联邦政府，折射出SpaceX在不到一年时间里经历的深刻转变。自SpaceX收购马斯克旗下AI公司xAI以来，这家曾长期依赖NASA和美国国防部合同的火箭公司，正迅速向AI算力服务商靠拢。 据SpaceX文件显示，第三季度仅有两名客户的营收占比超过总营收的10%。 除Anthropic外，另一客户（可能为多个政府机构的合计付款）在第三季度仅占营收的16.6%，而该客户在2025年的占比约为五分之一。 马斯克还预测，曾是SpaceX最重要合作伙伴之一的NASA，其付款在2026年将占公司营收不足5%。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 报道：欧洲央行官员倾向12月加息，通胀前景是关键变量
articles.summary: 若通胀形势未能改善，欧洲央行将在12月重启加息——这一信号正推动市场对年内再度收紧货币政策的预期持续升温。 据彭博援引知情人士透露， 欧洲央行官员普遍认为，综合当前数据及中东战争对经济的冲击，可能需要再加息25个基点以遏制通胀 。知情人士要求匿名，理由是相关讨论属于内部事项。 市场对此已有所定价， 当前交易显示12月再度加息25个基点的概率约为85%，且投资者预期紧缩周期将延续至2027年，届时或至少再有一次行动。 本周按兵不动，但加息方向"明确" 欧洲央行本周维持存款利率于2.5%不变，这是自伊朗战争冲击能源市场、推动通胀飙升至2%目标近两倍以来的第三次利率决议。 行长拉加德宣布将提前卸任，此消息在一定程度上盖过了本次决议本身的焦点，但她仍明确表示，利率的走向"清晰可辨"。 拉加德透露，本周会议上确曾讨论加息方案，随后官员们才选择按兵不动。知情人士透露，本周内部讨论"极为激烈"。 2.5%的存款利率处于货币政策被认定对经济呈中性效果的区间上限。 通胀风险偏上行，经济增长压力显现 在通胀判断上， 拉加德虽淡化了价格压力向能源领域以外扩散的风险 ，但同时强调上行风险仍是主要倾向；相比之下，经济增长面临的风险方向则相反——增长不及预期的隐忧正在加大。 预计周五公布的数据将显示，三季度经济增速从二季度的0.6%放缓至0.2%，尽管二季度数据因爱尔兰的亮眼表现而明显抬高了基数。与此同时，消费者价格涨幅预计将从3.8%加速至3.9%。 分析人士：紧缩周期或已接近尾声 彭博经济学家David Powell和Simona Delle Chiaie认为，"管理委员会正在为终结本轮紧缩周期奠定基础，尽管欧洲央行为12月再次加息留有余地。" 两位分析师表示，拉加德近期的表态进一步强化了他们的判断——其言论更多强调能源冲击外溢效应的有限迹象，以及金融条件收紧的效果。 知情人士同时提醒，目前尚无任何决定，局势可能迅速生变，尤其是鉴于中东局势发展难以预判。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 大空头Eisman质疑Anthropic"非常刻意"隐瞒最新财报，AI安全叙事遭遇信任危机
articles.summary: 《大空头》原型人物Steve Eisman公开质疑Anthropic，他称这家寻求约2万亿美元估值的企业，"非常刻意"地隐瞒了最新季度财务数据。 10月28日周三，Eisman在《Prof G Markets》播客中质问： Anthropic于10月26日提交的招股书，财务数据为何仅截至6月 。当被问及这一遗漏是否属故意时，他只答了一句： 只能说非常刻意。 他援引路透数据指出， Anthropic季度营收增速已从二季度的144%降至三季度的45%。据播客及Yahoo援引的更近期信息，其"爆炸性增长"可能正在失去动力。 Eisman同时指出，公司创造营收的经济模型也出现明显恶化迹象，而这些信息正是被排除在招股文件之外的内容。 指控来源：以预见次贷危机著称的知名投资者 Steve Eisman因在《大空头》中被刻画为提前识破次贷危机而声名大噪，其职业声誉建立于识别华尔街普遍忽视的金融荒谬之上。 Eisman的核心质疑在于：Anthropic的招股文件截止日期为10月26日，却仅涵盖至6月底的财务数据，这意味着市场在评估该公司近2万亿美元估值时，所依据的财务信息存在至少一个完整季度的空白。 Eisman进一步指出，公司在营收增速放缓的同时，其产生收入的成本结构也在恶化，这使得财务画面较招股说明书所呈现的更为复杂。 此次争议的核心，是AI领域高企估值与实际财务表现之间日益扩大的落差。Anthropic拥有庞大的基础设施资本承诺，且持续处于亏损状态，若其最新数据显示增长势头已经减弱，则支撑近2万亿美元估值的增长假设将面临直接挑战。 目前Anthropic尚未就上述指控公开回应。 对于潜在投资者而言，Eisman的质疑意味着在正式IPO前，公司的最新季度财务透明度将成为关键审查焦点。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 10月30日会员早报：Alphabet遭遇上市以来最惨一日 AI投资推动美国三季度经济增速升至3.4%
articles.summary: 1、【Alphabet遭遇上市以来最惨一日】Alphabet于10月28日美股收盘后发布财报。三季度营收同比增长25%，至1276亿美元，略低于分析师预期的1282亿美元；净利润同比下降约25%至262亿美元，每股收益2.12美元，远低于约3美元的市场预期，这是公司近四年来首次营收与利润双双不及预期。搜索收入不及预期，部分原因在于用户在“AI模式”下发起的查询，从广告中赚到的钱更少。消息重新点燃了市场对Alphabet等公司在AI上砸下巨资的担忧，以科技股为主的纳斯达克综合指数下跌逾1%。 2、【AI投资推动美国三季度经济增速升至3.4%】美国商务部经济分析局（BEA）10月29日公布初步估计。数据显示，第三季度美国实际GDP按年率计算增长3.4%，二季度为2.2%。这是2025年三季度以来最快的增速，也高于路透调查预期的3.2%。投资是本季度增长的最大来源。私人国内投资贡献了3.27个百分点。其中企业设备投资按年率增长20.9%，为2020年三季度以来最快，贡献1.16个百分点，是六年来最多。在设备投资之外，信息处理设备投资激增37.4%，软件和研发投资分别增长9.6%和7.5%。 3、【美国9月PCE通胀升至3.6%创5月以来新高】美国商务部经济分析局（BEA）当地时间10月29日公布的数据显示，美国9月个人消费支出（PCE）物价指数同比上涨3.6%，符合市场预期，高于前值3.4%，为今年5月以来最高；环比上涨0.5%，同样符合预期。剔除食品和能源的核心PCE物价指数同比上涨3.1%，前值3.0%，也是四个月来高点。 4、【美国外卖龙头DoorDash拟斥资170亿美元收购Instacart】美国最大的餐饮外卖平台DoorDash周四宣布，已与Instacart（上市主体为Maplebear）达成最终协议，以约170亿美元收购这家生鲜杂货配送巨头，这是DoorDash迄今规模最大的一笔交易。亚马逊和沃尔玛这两位电商老将近来都把线上生鲜杂货订单列为重点，此次收购将增强DoorDash与之抗衡的实力。 5、【拉加德将提前九个月卸任欧洲央行行长】欧洲央行行长克里斯蒂娜·拉加德将于明年2月卸任，比八年任期届满提前约九个月。这一决定在外界猜测数月后正式宣布，将引发欧洲央行成立28年来规模最大的领导层洗牌之一，而此时欧元区通胀压力正再度抬头。西班牙和荷兰已各自力挺本国一位前央行行长接替她。

articles.title: 力拓ADR一度跌超4%：蒙古奥尤陶勒盖铜矿发生岩崩事故，地下运营暂停
articles.summary: 力拓股价周四下跌，旗下位于蒙古国南部的奥尤陶勒盖铜矿发生岩崩事故，造成15名工人受伤。彭博报道称，该矿已暂时关闭地下运营，事故后续影响受到关注。 新华社周四报道称，奥尤陶勒盖铜矿当地时间10月29日18时左右发生岩崩事故。 矿场运营方奥尤陶勒盖有限责任公司表示，矿区井下岩石破碎带突发震动性地质事件，引发局部岩崩，现场作业人员受到波及。事故造成15名工人受伤，目前暂无人员死亡报告。 事故发生后，运营方启动应急处置机制，对受伤工人开展医疗检查与救治，伤者伤情整体平稳。运营方表示，仍在对事故成因及现场安全状况进行全面评估。 彭博援引知情人士报道称，该矿暂时关闭地下运营；截至目前，事故造成的具体停产时长及对产量的影响尚不明确。 力拓ADR周四盘中一度跌超4%，创3月以来新低，随后小幅反弹，截至发稿下跌3.21%。 周四铜价下跌，媒体报道事故发生后短线跳涨，后有所回落，截至发稿，纽约铜下跌1.07%。 全球大型铜矿之一，地下业务是重要增长引擎 奥尤陶勒盖是全球规模最大的铜矿之一，采用露天开采与地下开采并行的模式。力拓持有该矿66%的股权并负责运营管理，蒙古国政府持有其余34%的股权。 该矿也是力拓未来铜产量增长的重要来源。力拓此前表示，奥尤陶勒盖露天矿与地下矿在2028年至2036年期间，预计年均铜产量可达约50万吨。 矿山地下生产于2023年启动，随着地下采矿逐步爬坡，该项目在力拓铜业务中的重要性持续提升。 此次事故发生后，地下运营暂时关闭，矿山何时恢复正常作业，以及安全评估是否会影响后续生产进度，成为值得关注的问题。目前尚无足够信息判断此次事故将对力拓全年铜产量或长期产量目标造成多大影响。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
